title: Sewershed Chemical Fingerprinting to Trace PFAS Sources
one_liner: A network of automated samplers plus non-target mass-spectrometry that bisects a city's sewer tree to find which industrial sources are putting PFAS into the plant.
customer: Wastewater utilities with biosolids or effluent PFAS problems, industrial pretreatment coordinators, state PFAS programs (Michigan's industrial pretreatment PFAS initiative is a precedent, from my background knowledge), and industrial dischargers that want an independent baseline. The utility or state pays.
problem: Wastewater plants cannot remove PFAS, yet they receive it from platers, landfills, textile, paper and semiconductor users, and they inherit the biosolids and effluent liability. Utilities treat sources as unknowable, so they cannot enforce or recover cost. Europe's polluter-pays wastewater rules will also need load attribution.
solution: Install 10-30 autosamplers per sewershed (pump stations and manholes). Analyze weekly composites through a partner lab using high-resolution mass spectrometry, total organofluorine and precursor assays. Use ML on the network tree to attribute loads to upstream sub-catchments, then deliver a source map and enforcement-grade evidence. First product: a 12-week campaign.
why_now: The 2027 monitoring wave, biosolids scrutiny, and falling costs of high-resolution mass spectrometry plus the COVID-era playbook for sewer-network sampling all converge.
revenue_model: $120-300k per campaign, $60-150k/yr surveillance subscriptions, and cost-recovery success fees.
non_obvious_insight: A sewer network is a tree, so 15 samplers can bisect to a source in weeks, like contact tracing. The buyer is the utility's legal and finance side seeking cost recovery from polluters, not the environmental regulator.
first_30_days: Sign one small city or regional plant with a known biosolids problem, or a state program. Partner with a commercial lab that has non-target capability instead of buying instruments. Run a pilot at eight nodes and produce a source-bisection map.

title: GLP-1 Size-Curve Index for Apparel Planners
one_liner: A monthly 'size-shift index' that tells merchandise planners, airlines and furniture makers how GLP-1 adoption is moving their customers' bodies.
customer: Merchandise planners and size-curve analysts at apparel, footwear and outdoor brands and off-price retailers, plus airline, cruise, furniture and medical-equipment planners.
problem: Households with a GLP-1 user doubled to ~22%, and users lose double-digit percentages of body weight in a year. Retailers still plan size curves on last year's sell-through, which lags, causing markdowns on the wrong sizes. CFOs are already modeling downstream effects (Jefferies estimates ~$600M/yr airline fuel savings).
solution: Build an index by region, age and gender from licensed or partner data (pharmacy-fill proxies where affordable, retailer size and returns data, sizing surveys, public health data) and forecast size-curve migration by category. Deliver an API, a quarterly briefing, and a custom-model add-on.
why_now: Adoption accelerated after the 2026 pill launches. BCG and GoodRx data show measurable spend shifts (less pasta and bakery, more fragrance, skincare and supplements), so consumer-goods planners are hunting for leading indicators.
revenue_model: $40-120k/year per retailer or brand, plus $20-60k custom-modeling projects.
non_obvious_insight: Sell-through is a lagging indicator, and the drug adoption curve by ZIP is a leading one. It is a healthcare-adjacent data business with no clinical regulation if built on aggregated data, so a two-person team can sell it to non-healthcare budgets.
first_30_days: Build v0 from public data (NHANES, BRFSS, Google Trends) plus a 2,000-person sizing survey. Email 30 planners with a free size-shift report for one category and offer partner-data-in-exchange pricing. Sign one $15k pilot.

title: L-Band Radar Watchdog for Small Levee Districts
one_liner: Turn free NISAR L-band radar into monthly, engineer-stamped settlement and seepage alerts for the small local districts that own most of America's levees.
customer: Reclamation, levee and drainage districts (California Delta and Central Valley, Iowa/Illinois/Missouri/Arkansas drainage districts) and owners of small high-hazard earthen dams and irrigation canals. Budgets are $50k to $2M a year, run by a board plus a part-time manager.
problem: Grass-covered earthen levees lose coherence in C-band InSAR (Sentinel-1), so cheap remote settlement monitoring never worked on them. Districts rely on annual walk-through inspections by volunteers or consultants. Failures are catastrophic, and grant, subvention and insurance paperwork demands documented condition history that most districts lack.
solution: A pipeline on NISAR L-band (about 10 m, 12-day repeat, which sees through vegetation) plus Sentinel-1 and soil-moisture change. It produces per-levee-mile maps of slumping, settlement and unusual wetness (seepage proxy). Alerts go to a partner licensed geotechnical engineer, who signs a one-page condition letter. The district attaches that letter to state levee-subvention and federal rehabilitation-program files, insurer renewals and board minutes. The dashboard is secondary; the stamped trigger is the product.
why_now: NASA/ISRO began releasing NISAR L-band data free through ASF DAAC on July 20, 2026 (acquisitions from June 17, 2026; full science record due by end of 2026). Tens of thousands of levee miles are locally owned, and nobody had L-band time series at this cadence before. Whoever starts the baseline now owns the longest history.
revenue_model: Subscription of $3k to $8k a year per district, tiered by levee miles. Add $1.5k to $4k per engineer-stamped event report. Later, portfolio-level data licences to flood insurers and reinsurers, and to state agencies that fund many districts.
non_obvious_insight: The radar data is free and commoditizing, so the data is not what the customer buys. They buy a defensible, professionally signed trigger that unlocks grant money, satisfies insurers and shifts liability. The moat is the engineer-of-record relationship, local ground truth and a baseline archive that starts accumulating today.
first_30_days: Process Sentinel-1, ALOS-2 and the first NISAR stacks over one Delta island or Iowa drainage district with a known past slump, to show a retrospective catch. Sign a geotech firm as engineer of record. Offer 5 districts a free baseline map and a $1.5k pilot, pitched at levee-district association and flood-board meetings. Aim for 2 paid pilots by day 30.

title: Flood Cover Sold to the Lender
one_liner: Homeowners won't buy flood insurance, but the bank holding their mortgage should, because the uninsured flood loss lands on the lender's collateral.
customer: Community banks, credit unions and non-bank mortgage servicers with concentrated mortgage exposure outside FEMA high-risk zones, where flood cover isn't mandatory.
problem: Moody's puts uninsured US flood exposure at $375B-$1T. Private flood capacity is growing but 'customers aren't buying' (Insurance Business, 2026-07-22). Outside mandatory-purchase zones, borrowers skip cover, then walk or go delinquent after a flood and leave the lender with damaged collateral.
solution: Two steps. First, a parcel-level flood-exposure audit of the lender's book. Second, a lender-paid group or blanket flood policy (indemnity with a parametric fast-pay component) for the highest-risk non-mandatory loans, with disclosure and an opt-out. It is delivered as an MGA program on existing private flood capacity, and regulatory structure is validated state by state.
why_now: Private flood capacity is expanding (Neptune passed 300k policies and $400M premium). Reinsurance is softening, so capacity is cheap. Record cat bond issuance ($65.6B outstanding) shows abundant capital, and bank regulators are asking about climate concentration.
revenue_model: MGA commission and policy fees (roughly 10-20% of premium) plus a $15k-$40k paid portfolio audit per lender.
non_obvious_insight: The demand problem is really a distribution problem. Selling to 10,000 skeptical homeowners is expensive, while selling to one lender covers thousands of borrowers. The party with the incentive to buy is the one who bears the unmandated loss.
first_30_days: Run free flood-exposure audits for 20 credit unions in river and Gulf states using public mortgage data and open flood models. Line up a licensed surplus-lines partner. Sell one paid pilot covering about 500 highest-risk loans.

title: Model-of-Origin Forensics for AI Music Catalogs
one_liner: Attribute a track to the generator and version that made it, so catalog owners and litigators can separate legacy unlicensed-model output from the rest.
customer: Distributors, sync and production-music libraries, entertainment law firms and insurers, plus brand legal teams clearing ad music.
problem: Suno replaced its models on Sep 9 with one trained on licensed music, after label suits. A second UMG/Sony suit over roughly 60k songs is reported (single source, verify). Warner settled. Tens of millions of tracks from older models are already distributed or embedded in videos and ads. Downstream legal exposure is unproven, but risk-averse counsel will want to know which tracks came from which model. Deezer's detector answers 'AI or not,' and is licensed only to platforms.
solution: A classifier and evidence report attributing audio to a generator family and version range (Suno, Udio, Stable Audio, ElevenLabs Music and others), trained on labeled corpora we generate ourselves from paid subscriptions to each version. Output: family, version range, confidence, and whether a post-Aug 6 Suno watermark is present. Includes catalog-level exposure heat maps, a batch API, and expert-witness-ready reports.
why_now: Suno's Sep 9 model swap and Aug 6 watermarking pledge create a hard before-and-after line. Pre-watermark, pre-swap tracks are exactly the legacy tail that needs forensic attribution, and the lawsuits make the question urgent.
revenue_model: $0.05-0.25 per track for batch screening, $5-50k per catalog audit, $15-75k per litigation-grade report, and annual retainers for law firms and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is building 'AI or not' detectors, which are crowded and sell at consumer prices ($20/month). Nobody sells 'which model, which version, before or after the licensed swap.' That is the question that maps to legal liability, so it prices like legal risk.
first_30_days: Subscribe to the major generators and produce about 5k labeled tracks per version. Get a baseline classifier working in three weeks. Approach five sync libraries and two boutique entertainment-law firms, and sell $10k pilot audits of a 20k-track catalog subset.

title: Reuse Exchange for Closing Parish Contents
one_liner: A cataloging, canon-law compliance and matching service that moves stained glass, statues, vestments, bells and furniture from closing parishes to churches that need them.
customer: Dioceses and archdiocesan closure committees, religious orders and denominational property offices, with receiving parishes, new chapels and immigrant or missionary congregations on the other side.
problem: Closure committees catalog contents by hand, and surplus goes out through liturgical dealers. Sacred items risk profane use (confessionals turned into restaurant phone booths, upsetting donors' families), canon law restricts profane sale, and organs and murals often cannot be saved.
solution: A photo-cataloging app with AI-assisted identification, provenance and donor-plaque tracking, blessed-status and canon-law flags, and a bishop approval workflow. A gated marketplace of vetted receiving churches, including overseas missions served by consolidated containers. Optionally digitally sample condemned organs before removal.
why_now: Parish consolidations continue while church attendance is flat (Pew: 33% attend monthly). Dioceses are cash-strapped and want revenue from contents. Photo AI and container consolidation are now cheap.
revenue_model: A per-closure project fee ($5-25k), 10-15% commission on sales, and a freight-consolidation margin on overseas shipments.
non_obvious_insight: Buyers are not the scarce input. Trust and compliance are: sellers need proof items will not be profaned, and buyers in growing regions need provenance and affordable freight. A vetted receiving-church network is the asset incumbents (liturgical dealers) lack.
first_30_days: Offer 3 diocesan property offices a free catalog of one closing church. Build a list of 50 missionary and immigrant-parish buyers through religious-order mission offices. Ship the first container.

title: Placement Exchange for Clients PE Firms Shed
one_liner: A compliant offboarding and warm-handoff service that places small clients dropped by PE-backed accounting firms with vetted independent bookkeepers.
customer: PE-backed and roll-up accounting platforms that raise fee minimums and prune small clients, and independent bookkeepers, enrolled agents and CPAs who want more clients.
problem: PE roll-ups push firms toward larger clients (prior knowledge, not re-verified), so thousands of micro-clients get a 30-day termination letter with scattered records. The exiting firm has E&O and reputation exposure, and the clients don't know where to go. Independent shops want clients but cannot find or vet them. CPA supply is flat at about 678,000.
solution: An offboarding workflow for the shedding firm: client consent, export of prior-year returns and workpapers, engagement-letter templates, and a warm handoff to independents matched on industry, software, language and location. Receiving firms are vetted and rated, and there is a service-level guarantee if the client is unhappy.
why_now: Multi-year PE consolidation of accounting firms continues, AI reduces cost-to-serve for large clients faster than small ones, and the CPA pipeline is flat while demand is projected to rise.
revenue_model: $150-400 per placed client from the receiving firm, $50-100 per client offboarding fee from the shedding firm, and later 8-10% of first-year fees as a recurring referral.
non_obvious_insight: For the roll-up, shedding small clients is an unpriced cost center with legal exposure, so it will pay for graceful exits. The demand side is a waiting list of independents.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 independent bookkeepers and EAs as the buyer panel. Approach operations leaders at five regional roll-ups and offer a free pilot for 50 pruned clients. Build the export checklist and record acceptance and satisfaction rates.

title: Transition Sponsor Radar for Strategic Breakthrough Awards
one_liner: A subscription and dossier service that maps each SBIR Phase II technology to the specific budget line, program office and person who could commit to a Program Objective Memorandum (POM), which the new $30M Strategic Breakthrough awards require.
customer: Phase II awardees in DoD-funded SBIR (thousands per year) that want Phase III or Strategic Breakthrough money, plus SBIR-focused VCs and advisors who decide which portfolio companies to back.
problem: Strategic Breakthrough awards run up to $30M over 48 months, but a company needs at least one prior Phase II, at least 100% matching funds from new private capital or non-SBIR government money, and, for DoD, a 'commitment for inclusion in a program objective memorandum' from the acquisition executive or higher. Agencies must contract within 90 days of a proposal. The technology is rarely the bottleneck. The bottleneck is finding the one person with authority over a budget line, and knowing the POM calendar, since the POM is written 18 to 24 months ahead of the fiscal year. The public data (R-1/R-2 RDT&E exhibits, P-1 procurement lines, FPDS contracts, SBIR.gov awards) exists but is not indexed by technology.
solution: Build a searchable graph linking SBIR.gov Phase II abstracts to R-2 program elements, project numbers and named PEOs/PMs, and to FPDS Phase III contracts (where SBIR data-rights clauses appear). For each customer, produce a 'sponsor dossier': the top 5 program elements that could absorb the tech, the POM cycle dates, who to call, precedent Phase III transitions, and candidate match-fund sources. Add a monthly alert when a relevant program element grows or a new Phase III model contract appears.
why_now: The Strategic Breakthrough allocation (up to 0.50% of an agency's R&D budget where R&D exceeds $100M) takes effect in FY2026 and runs to September 30, 2031. Agencies must also create standardized Phase I/II/III model contracts and track direct-to-Phase-II, strategic breakthrough and Phase III awards in the database. Data on where transitions happen will become far richer as this reporting starts.
revenue_model: $12k to $20k per tech-specific sponsor dossier, paid partly from the $50k Phase II T&BA allowance. $1,500 per month subscription for alerts and updates. $5k per month for SBIR-focused VC funds screening deals. Success fee on Phase III wins (1% to 3%) as an optional add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is not funding, it is a named budget-holder who will put a line in a POM, and that map is buildable from public documents no one has joined to SBIR data. S. 3971 Section 3 (new Section 9(ff)(3)) sets the $30M cap, 48-month term, one prior Phase II, 100% match, DoD POM-commitment requirement and 90-day contracting deadline. Section 6 requires 'simplified and standardized procedures and model contracts' for Phase III. Section 8 requires the database to track Phase III prime and subcontract awards. All at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119s3971enr/html/BILLS-119s3971enr.htm. The award-size thresholds the SBA gave for April 2026 ($323,090 Phase I, $2,153,927 Phase II without SBA approval, https://www.sbir.gov/about) show how small the normal awards are next to a $30M award, so the sponsor commitment becomes the step everyone is scrambling for.
first_30_days: Download the SBIR.gov awards dataset and the latest DoD RDT&E R-2 exhibits (comptroller.defense.gov). Use an LLM to embed and match 200 recent Phase II abstracts to program elements, then have a former acquisition officer sanity-check the top matches. Give 10 Phase II founders a free one-page 'sponsor map' for their own tech. Convert 3 of them to a $12k dossier. Pitch 2 SBIR-focused VC funds a paid pilot on their portfolio.

title: Exit Desk for Orphaned Local-Marketing Assets
one_liner: A fixed-price service that finds, takes back and migrates the domain, listing, phone numbers and ad accounts locked inside shrinking legacy marketing vendors.
customer: Home-service and retail owners paying $200-1,200 a month to Yellow Pages descendants, marketing agencies and template-site hosts.
problem: Thryv's 2025 revenue was $785M and falling, with net income near $0.3M, so the vendor base is melting through price hikes, resales and shutdowns. Owners often do not own their domain, Google Business Profile admin rights, call-tracking numbers or ad accounts, and leaving means losing the phone number painted on the truck. Getting customers is still the top small-business challenge.
solution: A fixed-fee audit finds recurring vendor debits (via bank feed or bookkeeper), checks who owns each asset (WHOIS, GBP owner list, ad-account admin, tracking numbers), then executes the takeback: domain transfer, GBP ownership transfer, number port, site migration into an owner-owned stack, and contract cancellation notices. Optional monitoring alerts if a vendor re-takes control.
why_now: Legacy vendor decline is visible in public financials, AI site builders make replacement stacks cheap, and small businesses still need customers.
revenue_model: $299-799 one-time, $29/month monitoring, and referral fees from the destination stack (hosting, CRM, review tools).
non_obvious_insight: What the owner is paying for is a person who answers the phone, not leads. The exit is a control and trust problem more than a marketing problem. The bookkeeper sees the debit but has no workflow to end it.
first_30_days: Partner with 10 bookkeepers to flag legacy-vendor debits. Run 20 audits and publish a 'who owns your phone number' checklist to seed leads.

title: Transfer-Portal Durability Passport for College Athletes
one_liner: An athlete-owned, verified injury and load history that programs will demand before they commit six figures of revenue share.
customer: College programs (general managers, sports medicine, compliance), collectives and agents pay for verified dossiers; athletes get their file free and own it.
problem: Chain: the House settlement lets schools pay athletes up to about $20.5M in 2025-26, unlimited transfers and the June 2026 shift to a five-year eligibility clock make multi-year, money-bearing roster bets, yet there is no standard electronic medical record across schools. Injury history moves by phone call and rumor: athletes fear disclosure, programs fear buying a torn ACL, and agents cannot prove durability.
solution: A consent-based portal where athletes' athletic trainers upload structured injury and return-to-play summaries, a standardized functional battery (jump/landing, isometric strength, hop tests) run at partner performance gyms, and optional load history exports from Catapult or WHOOP. The athlete chooses who sees what; the receiving program pays for a standardized, verified dossier.
why_now: Revenue-share contracts, unlimited transfers and the 2026 eligibility overhaul raise the financial stakes of injuries; the proposed Protect College Sports Act would add post-eligibility medical coverage duties and privacy protections; state privacy laws and HIPRA push consent-based data handling.
revenue_model: $150-300 per verified passport paid by the receiving program; $10-25k per year per program for scouting and post-signing baselines; $99 per athlete from agents.
non_obvious_insight: The athlete, not the school, must own the file: that is what makes disclosure acceptable and gives buyers something they can trust. It is a Carfax for players, and the customers now have real money at risk.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 mid-major and D2 basketball and volleyball athletes entering the portal through 3-4 friendly agents, build the consent form and one-page dossier, run 10 test sessions at a local performance gym, and pitch three assistant coaches or GMs on paying $200 per dossier.

title: Loss-Draft Concierge for Disaster Rebuilds
one_liner: A draw desk that gets the insurance money for a destroyed house out of the mortgage servicer's restricted account and into the rebuild, paid by the contractors who need cash to start.
customer: Mortgaged homeowners whose houses were destroyed or damaged by fire, flood or storm pay $1,500-3,000 flat or about 1% of proceeds. Rebuild contractors pay 1.5-2.5% of each accelerated draw.
problem: When a mortgaged house is destroyed, insurance checks are made out to both the owner and the servicer. The servicer parks the money in a loss-draft account and releases it in inspection-gated stages, each requiring a contract, contractor license proof, permits, lien waivers, W-9s and photos. Homeowners cannot assemble the packet. Contractors will not start without money. Families pay rent and a mortgage on a lot with nothing on it. Rebuild fraud thrives in the gap.
solution: A draw desk that takes the servicer's letter and builds the draw packet in the exact format the servicer wants. It verifies the contractor's license, collects conditional and unconditional lien waivers on the state statutory forms, books inspections, submits, and chases weekly. It escalates to servicer executive complaint lines and state regulators. It ties every disbursement to milestone photos and waivers so the homeowner is protected from paying for work not done. It never holds the funds, which avoids money-transmitter issues. Later add bridge financing against expected draws.
why_now: The January 2025 Los Angeles fires destroyed roughly 16,000 structures and rebuilds are now at peak permit and construction paperwork. Storm and flood rebuilds continue in Texas, North Carolina and Florida, and every season adds more. Additional-living-expense coverage has clocks that expire, which makes delay costly. AI document handling makes lien-waiver, permit and inspection-photo checks cheap for a small team.
revenue_model: Flat rebuild-admin package or about 1% of proceeds from homeowners. A per-draw acceleration fee of 1.5-2.5% from contractors. Later, a spread on bridge loans and referral revenue from lenders and builders.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not the insurer. The money already exists and is locked behind paperwork the homeowner cannot produce. Public adjusters take about 10% to fight the insurer but nobody specializes in this second fight. The hidden buyer is the contractor, whose cash flow decides whether the site ever starts.
first_30_days: Join fire-survivor community groups and rebuild nonprofits in one affected area. Offer a free draw-packet review to the first 10 households. Sign 3 rebuild contractors whose draws are stalled. Charge a flat fee only after the first draw is released. Document days-to-funds before and after as your proof, then take the case studies to the next disaster market.

title: Smoke-and-Heat Escape Benefit for Remote Teams
one_liner: An employer-paid standby membership that, when smoke, heat-dome or evacuation triggers hit, moves remote employees within hours into pre-contracted hotel rooms with a tested desk and wifi outside the hazard zone.
customer: Heads of People or Business Continuity at remote-first companies of 150-2,000 staff (dev tools, fintech, SaaS, online education) where at least 15% of employees live in US West, Southwest, Gulf Coast or Canadian wildfire belts. They have no office to fall back on and a duty-of-care gap.
problem: When AQI hits 300, a heat dome coincides with a failed AC, or an evacuation order lands, remote employees improvise: sold-out hotels, price gouging, expense fights, lost work days. Corporate travel tools are built for planned trips, and consumer OTAs cannot guarantee inventory in an evacuation. Employers carry the productivity loss and the liability but have no product to buy.
solution: Employer buys standby access. Opted-in employees are monitored by home ZIP against public feeds (AQI forecasts, NWS extreme-heat warnings, evacuation zones, NHC cone). On a trigger the employee gets a one-tap offer: a confirmed room or extended-stay unit 100-400 miles away in a cleaner or cooler basin, at a pre-contracted rate, wifi speed-tested, pet and kid rules known, paid by virtual card. Hotels earn a small standby retainer on rooms held for trigger nights. Start with mid-tier and economy properties.
why_now: The 2026 travel market is K-shaped: mid and lower hotel tiers are pressured and booking windows shrank to about 33 days, so hoteliers will trade a discount for forward-committed revenue. Summer 2026 brought the hottest US July on record and a deadly European heatwave, making hazard seasons an HR planning assumption. Remote work is now normal enough that 'work from anywhere' relocation is a benefit line item, not an emergency.
revenue_model: $6-9 per employee per month for standby access and trigger monitoring, plus room nights at the contracted rate with about 12% platform margin. A 2,000-person employer is roughly $140-215K ARR before usage. Hotel-side retainer is funded out of the margin, not charged to hotels.
non_obvious_insight: Remote work turns evacuation from an unpredictable personal disaster into a budgetable HR benefit, because the worker's office travels with them. Smoke plumes and heat domes are regional and forecastable 24-72 hours out, so rooms can be bought as standby capacity instead of emergency spot inventory. Nobody sells this because benefits vendors do not touch hotel inventory and travel vendors do not monitor hazards.
first_30_days: Pick two hazard basins: Pacific Northwest/Northern California smoke, and Phoenix/Las Vegas heat. Handshake standby rates with 15-20 mid-tier hotels and extended-stay properties on both sides of each escape corridor. Recruit 3 remote-first startups through founder and People-ops Slack communities on a pay-per-activation pilot ($0 subscription for 60 days) with 30-50 opted-in employees each. Run it manually with a Slack bot, a spreadsheet and virtual cards. Publish a 'cost of a smoke day' calculator to generate leads.

title: Mobile Cobot Safety Validation Lab
one_liner: A van-based lab that measures collision forces and signs off robot and cobot cells against the 2025 ISO 10218 revisions.
customer: Cobot distributors, integrators and 10-200 person manufacturers deploying cells. EHS managers and insurers are the second buyers.
problem: North American robot orders are broadening into semiconductors, pharma and food, and cobots are 15.4% of units. The 2025 revisions of ISO 10218-1 and -2 (which absorbed the collaborative guidance of ISO/TS 15066) require documented risk assessment and validation. Few engineers can do it, and force-measurement gear costs tens of thousands of dollars. Distributors skip validation and the liability lands on the shop and its insurer.
solution: A van with a calibrated force and pressure measurement device, safety-scanner zone tester and stop-time tester. Technicians validate on site (contact-force mapping by body region, speed and separation checks) and deliver a signed report. Software stores and versions results for audits. Annual revalidation is a subscription.
why_now: Revised standards are in force, robot demand is broadening to small shops and new sectors, and mobile manipulators are coming into plants.
revenue_model: $2.5-6k per cell validation. White-label contracts with distributors. About $1.2k a year for revalidation. Referral fees from insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The limiting step for small-shop robots is fear of liability, not price. A third-party validation stamp is what insurers and owners want, and distributors have the incentive to sell but not the independence or equipment to certify.
first_30_days: Rent or buy a used force-measurement device. Sign three cobot distributors. Complete a machinery functional-safety credential. Validate the first five cells at a discount.

title: After-Death Home Reset for Hospice Families
one_liner: A two-person crew that returns the house to normal within 48 hours of a home hospice death: bed out, meds destroyed, room restored, memory box packed.
customer: Hospice agencies pay per home death, as a family-experience and bereavement differentiator. A second stream is families paying a premium, and funeral homes reselling it as an add-on.
problem: After a home death the hospital bed, oxygen concentrator and commode often sit in the living room for days. The DME vendor schedules pickup on its own clock. The leftover morphine, lorazepam and haloperidol 'comfort kit' sits in the fridge or cabinet. Nurses are supposed to see to disposal, but the home visit is often skipped or rushed, and families quietly keep or mis-dispose of them. The dead person's glasses, dentures and hearing aids end up in a drawer. The family remembers the empty bed in the middle of the room for the rest of their lives. The CAHPS Hospice family survey arrives months later and those last impressions color the answers.
solution: A chaplain-designed protocol delivered by two trained, background-checked staff in a branded van. On admission, the hospice photographs the room so the crew can restore the original furniture layout. Within 24 to 48 hours of death the crew coordinates or performs bed and equipment removal, destroys leftover controlled drugs with deactivation pouches and a witnessed log the hospice can put in the chart, and launders linens. They pack a memory box (glasses, jewelry, a worn shirt, the last handwritten note). They restore the room, open the windows, and offer a two-minute optional blessing or silence. A hand-off card tells the family what happens at 2 weeks and 6 weeks.
why_now: Hospice is consolidating, with private equity and large chains competing on public CAHPS-based quality scores that drive referrals. Regulators and communities are paying more attention to opioid diversion. Hospice per-diem margins are squeezed and the DME vendors they use are getting slower and cheaper. Home is where most hospice deaths occur. Also, nurses are stretched thin, so the care they used to give informally in that first day is disappearing, and nobody owns it.
revenue_model: Hospice pays $250 to $400 per home death on a per-case contract, with volume tiers. Families or funeral homes pay $450 to $600 for a premium version with a full room refresh and donation pickup for clothing and mobility aids. A hospice with roughly 100 patients on service has on the order of 25 to 35 deaths a month, around half at home, so three hospices support a small crew. Sponsorship from a nonprofit hospice foundation can cover indigent families.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the crisis is the moment of death. Insiders know the emotional injury persists in the physical room and in the loose ends nobody owns: the bed, the drugs, the dentures. The hospice would love to solve it but cannot bill for it and the nurse has already left. Whoever owns hours 6 through 48 after death, when the funeral home has taken the body and all clinical staff have gone, owns the family's memory of the hospice.
first_30_days: Sign one small nonprofit hospice as a design partner. Write the checklist with the chaplain, the DON and a pharmacist for the controlled-drug disposal log. Buy a used van, get general liability coverage, and hire two people with home-health-aide or hospitality backgrounds. Do the first 5 to 8 resets free in exchange for family feedback. Charge from case 9, and ask the hospice's quality director to compare family feedback scores with and without the reset.

title: Public-Access TV Stations Become Media Notaries
one_liner: Convert struggling PEG community-media centers into witnessed-recording and signing hubs that cities pay to certify official meeting video and creators pay to prove a recording was performed live by a human in a real room.
customer: City and county clerks ($300-600/month for signed, canonical video of meetings, hearings and emergency briefings), PEG access centers (keep about 60% as delivery partners), and local musicians, podcasters and hyperlocal news creators ($45 per witnessed session or $15/month for verified-clip embeds). Later buyers are sync buyers and ad agencies.
problem: PEG centers (public, educational and government access TV) are funded by cable franchise fees that erode as cable subscriptions fall (prior knowledge), yet they own studios, gear, staff and a role recording local government. Meanwhile fully AI tracks passed 50% of Deezer uploads (July 2026), AI-cloned officials' clips circulate, platform human badges are free and per-artist (Spotify) or absent (YouTube will not demote labeled AI), and detectors are only probabilistic. Nobody sells 'this was made live, in this room, on this date, witnessed by a public institution'.
solution: A roughly $600 witness kit plus software: hardware-signed capture into C2PA manifests, staff-attested session logs with an ID check of performers, and raw timestamped multitrack takes. Cities get a canonical signed meeting archive and a public 'verify this clip' page. Local news creators embed verified clips, and artists attach a 'Recorded live at [Center], [date]' credential to releases and distributor metadata.
why_now: EU AI Act Article 50 marking and disclosure duties started applying 2026-08-02. C2PA 2.3 and TikTok's July 2026 steering-committee entry mean signed media can now travel across platforms. Platforms went from tolerating to policing AI in months (Bandcamp ban, Spotify AI Persona labels, TIDAL demonetization), and PEG funding pressure means centers need new revenue lines.
revenue_model: City subscriptions, per-session fees split with PEG centers, an annual software license to centers, and later per-clip verification fees from sync buyers.
non_obvious_insight: A credential is only as trustworthy as the institution behind it. Platforms cannot referee because they sell AI tools, and detectors give probabilities while a witness gives testimony. PEG centers are the only neutral, government-adjacent, physically distributed and already-recording institutions in most towns, and their core asset is exactly what provenance lacks: a place and a person willing to attest.
first_30_days: Contact the Alliance for Community Media state chapters and equip 3 PEG stations in one state. Sign one month of council meetings free, then demo a deepfaked council clip against the signed original to sell a $300/month city plan. Open 'Witnessed Live' studio hours to 20 local artists at $45.

title: Tip Provenance Ledger for Tipped-Occupation Employers
one_liner: An evidence trail that classifies every dollar as a voluntary tip, service charge, pool or cash tip, to support new tip-deduction reporting.
customer: Restaurants, bars, salons, spas, barbershops, valet operators, car washes and delivery fleets with 5-60 workers on Toast, Square, Clover or spreadsheets, and self-employed booth renters in tipped occupations.
problem: The 2025 reconciliation law made qualified tips and overtime deductible, and the IRS says employers must file information returns on them. Workers now have an incentive to relabel pay as tips. Owners must separate voluntary tips from mandatory service charges, pooled tips and cash tips, and errors trigger worker disputes and IRS letters.
solution: Ingest POS, payment and payroll data and tag each dollar with provenance. Produce the W-2 or 1099 support schedule, worker-facing statements so employees can claim their deduction, and an audit binder. Flag anomalies such as a service charge quietly recategorized as tips at year-end.
why_now: Tax year 2026 is the first full year under the new rules and W-2s are due January 31, 2027. Payroll vendors are adding fields but not provenance.
revenue_model: $29-79 per location per month, plus $3 per worker statement. Channel through POS app stores and restaurant bookkeepers.
non_obvious_insight: A deduction that is valuable to both worker and owner creates an incentive to reclassify, which makes the evidence trail the product, in the same way that exemption certificates support sales-tax deductions. Payroll vendors will add a field but not the audit trail.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 restaurants and salons through bookkeepers. Build a Square and Toast CSV importer and offer a free Q4 tip audit. Convert audit customers to an annual plan ahead of the W-2 deadline.

title: Surety-Bonded License Plates for AI Agents
one_liner: A registrar that binds each autonomous agent to a legally accountable, insured principal through a surety bond and a revocable credential merchants and platforms can check.
customer: Agent developers and vendors that need acceptance by merchants, booking and B2B procurement platforms, the merchants and platforms that want to admit agents safely, and surety insurers or MGAs.
problem: Visa, Mastercard and Amex are activating agent payments in 2026, but dispute and liability infrastructure barely exists. Merchants bear the chargebacks, and Mastercard is reportedly planning scheme-carried liability for certified agents. Identity schemes such as Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol and Cloudflare's signed agents say who an agent is, but not who pays when it misbehaves.
solution: Register the agent and underwrite it with a test suite, spend caps and a behaviour policy. Issue a signed credential with a visible bond limit, and let merchants and platforms verify it with one API call. A claims process pays merchants for agent-caused losses, and violations revoke the credential. Start with an MGA and fronting-carrier partnership.
why_now: Card networks are moving on agent payments in 2026, Lloyd's-backed AI liability covers launched in 2025, and merchants are asking who is liable for agent orders. Signed-agent identity standards exist, so the missing layer is accountability.
revenue_model: Annual premium of 1-5% of bond limit, a registration fee, and float on the claims reserve.
non_obvious_insight: Identity without liability is theatre. The mature trust machine for strangers who might not pay is suretyship (contractor licences, notary bonds), not a reputation score, and a bond turns 'trust me' into a price.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical (restaurant and hotel booking, or B2B procurement agents). Sign five agent developers, secure a letter of intent from a surety or MGA, build the underwriting test suite, and get three merchants to trial a bonded-only allowlist.

title: Dr. Simi USA: Pharmacy-Plus-Consult for the Uninsured
one_liner: Small-format, generic-first pharmacies with a nurse-practitioner consult room beside the counter, posted cash prices and no insurance needed, following Mexico's Farmacias Similares model and landing in US pharmacy deserts.
customer: Uninsured and underinsured adults in pharmacy deserts and immigrant neighborhoods. An estimated 4.8M Americans lost coverage after the enhanced ACA subsidies expired, and about 48M people live in pharmacy deserts. The second customer is at-risk independent pharmacists who license the clinic kit.
problem: Rite Aid is gone (all stores closed after its 2025 Chapter 11), Walgreens is shrinking, and independents are squeezed by PBM reimbursement. An uninsured person with a UTI or sinus infection faces a $150-250 urgent-care visit plus retail drug prices, so many just skip treatment.
solution: An 800-1,200 sq ft store or a 200 sq ft conversion inside an existing independent pharmacy. A flat $25-40 NP consult (loss leader), point-of-care tests (strep, flu, UTI, A1c), on-site dispensing of generics at transparent cost-plus prices, bilingual staff, and chronic-refill programs. The visit and the dispense happen in one 10-minute stop, so there is no abandoned prescription. Mexico's Farmacias Similares runs thousands of outlets with an attached doctor's office charging a few dollars.
why_now: Coverage is shrinking at the same time as pharmacy access: enhanced ACA subsidies lapsed at the end of 2025, Medicaid cuts phase in through 2026-27, and Rite Aid's liquidation left holes in low-income neighborhoods. Cost Plus Drugs has taught Americans to expect transparent generic prices, so a cash-price store is no longer strange.
revenue_model: Dispensing margin on generics, flat consult fees, point-of-care lab fees, OTC sales, plus licensing or franchise fees for the turnkey clinic-in-a-pharmacy kit sold to independents.
non_obvious_insight: Don't compete with telehealth on convenience; win on adjacency. Consult plus dispense in one stop removes the biggest leak in cash-pay care, which is people who get a prescription and never fill it. The fastest route isn't building stores at all. It is converting existing independents on the edge of closure by giving them a second revenue line, and an already-licensed pharmacy removes months of setup.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 independent pharmacies in Latino neighborhoods (Texas, Florida or Illinois). Contract per-diem NPs under a collaborative practice agreement, build a 100 sq ft consult room, and print a simple price list ('$29 visit, $4 generics'). Market through WhatsApp groups, churches and community radio. Run a 60-day pilot and track visit-to-fill conversion and margin per visit.

title: Neutral Noise-and-Flight Monitors for Drone Hubs
one_liner: Independent noise and flight-log monitoring that gives cities and neighbors a referee for drone-delivery hub permits, and gives operators and retail hosts approvable evidence.
customer: Drone-delivery operators and the retailers hosting hubs at store sites, paying to win and keep permits. City planning departments and neighborhood groups are the audience.
problem: Cities cannot regulate flight paths but can zone launch hubs. Northglenn requires a special-use permit, a 200 ft residential buffer and 65 dB at the property line. Wing and Walmart target 270+ sites by 2027 and Lowe's launched on Sep 28, 2026, so each site needs a hearing. Neighbors distrust operator-supplied noise data, cities lack staff and gear to check 65 dB, and a $5k-$15k consultant noise study is one-off and stale on day one.
solution: A permit-ready package. Before the application, a 7-day baseline at the property lines with calibrated low-cost acoustic sensors. After launch, continuous monitoring, tamper-evident logs, a public dashboard and alerts, matched to operator flight logs to attribute each event. An annual certification report cities can write into conditions of approval. Complaint triage: 'was a drone there at 3:14 pm? yes, 62 dB, within limit.'
why_now: The retail-scale rollout (Walmart/Wing 270+ sites, Lowe's/Wing/DoorDash launch on Sep 28, 2026, Zipline past 2M deliveries) is hitting local ground rules. Amazon paused after an Oct 2025 crane collision, so safety and trust are sensitive. Cities are drafting rules now.
revenue_model: $1,500 baseline and report per site. $300-$600/mo per site for monitoring, dashboard and certification. Optional city-charged permit fee. The city chooses the vendor, and raw data is public to protect neutrality.
non_obvious_insight: Local permitting, not the FAA, is the binding constraint on drone-delivery rollout. The currency of permits is neighbor trust, so a neutral measurement with a public dashboard is worth more than a better noise model. The party both sides accept as referee wins, and the fee is paid by whoever needs approval. Conflict-of-interest guards are the product: public raw data, no success fees, a firewall from operators.
first_30_days: Buy 10 sensors and calibrate them. Pick 3 cities with active hub hearings. Offer a free baseline for one live application at a store site. Get a city planner to reference the method in conditions of approval. Sign the first paid contract with a retail host or operator. Aim for 15-30 monitored sites by month 6.

title: Driver's Ed for Smartphones, Sold to Parent Groups
one_liner: Ten-week, cohort-based 'phone license' programs where a whole grade's parents and kids pledge together, kids earn tiered device access through in-person challenges, and the finish is a coming-of-age ceremony.
customer: Parent groups for one grade at one school (PTA/PTO, church youth groups, scout troops, neighborhoods) with kids aged 9-13 facing the first-smartphone decision. Parents pay about $249 per child. PTAs get a rev-share. Later: device partners and employers offering parent benefits.
problem: The first smartphone is a collective-action problem ('everyone else has one'). Parental-control software fails technically (7 in 10 Australian under-16s reportedly still hold accounts) and socially. The first phone has become an unguided adolescent initiation with no ritual, no community and no meaning, while loneliness among the young is rising.
solution: 1) A Parent Pact night to agree shared rules. 2) Ten weekly 90-minute kid sessions with trained youth facilitators covering boredom, friendship, spotting manipulative design, AI-companion literacy and group-chat etiquette, with badges earned in person. 3) Tiered device 'licenses': none, then dumbphone or watch, then a filtered smartphone using OS-level age signals, then full access, each unlocked at cohort milestones with parent sign-off. 4) A License Ceremony with families. 5) An alumni circle with monthly meetups and a parent forum.
why_now: Under-16 bans (Australia Dec 2025, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Florida) and app-store or OS-level age-assurance laws (California's Digital Age Assurance Act, Texas) are tiering the internet by age. Roblox now tiers by age (Kids, Select, standard). Support for Australia's ban has fallen to 57% and enforcement is leaky, so parents need a home-side complement. Twelve US states have school phone bans.
revenue_model: About $249 per child per cohort, a 15% rev-share to PTAs, bounties on tier-appropriate device or plan activations (verify what partners will pay), a $600 facilitator certification for teachers and youth workers, and later employer-paid parent benefits.
non_obvious_insight: The first smartphone fails as a family decision but works as a class decision. Because the product synchronizes a social graph, its moat is the cohort, not code. And a secular rite of passage supplies the 'meaning' that makes kids willing, which content-filtering apps cannot provide.
first_30_days: Pilot with two elementary schools' 4th- and 5th-grade parent groups through PTA presidents and 'Wait Until 8th' pledge lists. Recruit four facilitators (education or psychology students and retired coaches). Charge $249, run cohorts October-December so graduation lands before holiday phone gifting, and track how many kids stay phone-free until 13.

title: Guaranteed Midday Walker as Apartment Amenity
one_liner: Sell apartment operators a fixed on-site walker window as a renewal and lease-up amenity, with residents paying a discounted per-walk fee and the building paying a retainer.
customer: Owners and property managers of 150 to 500 unit multifamily buildings in dense metros, paying a monthly retainer. Residents are the secondary payers.
problem: A solo walker loses 35 to 45 percent of the paid day to driving between homes, parking, and building lobbies. Buildings, meanwhile, pay quietly for dogs: barking and noise complaints, damage from anxious dogs, waste on the property, and hidden-dog lease violations. Pet owners renew at higher rates than other tenants, but it is hard to monetize them with pet rent, especially where fees are capped or scrutinized.
solution: A walker holds fixed weekday windows (for example 11am to 2pm and 5 to 7pm) in the building, using the fob and package room. Residents book by QR code or text, and the walker walks compatible dogs from nearby floors in groups of 3 to 4 (dog compatibility is something a walker learns quickly), with a lobby handoff. Yield per hour roughly doubles or triples versus door-to-door, so residents pay about $12 to $15 per walk instead of $25 to $30. The building gets a monthly report on walks completed, incidents, and waste-bag use, plus marketing copy ('guaranteed midday walk') for lease-up and renewals. I could not confirm in this session whether a comparable product already operates at scale, so check competitors first.
why_now: Return-to-office mandates put more dogs alone midday. Big multifamily supply waves in many metros mean operators compete on concessions and retention, and are shifting amenity spend from gyms to services. Pet-fee restrictions in some states and cities push operators to bundle services instead of charging rent. Simple text-and-QR booking removes the back-office cost that used to make this unprofitable.
revenue_model: Building retainer of roughly $1,500 to $3,000 a month for guaranteed windows, plus resident per-walk fees of $12 to $15, plus optional add-ons (waste station servicing, dog-friendly move-in tours). Expand by selling to regional operators as a portfolio amenity program.
non_obvious_insight: The walker's real margin killer is geography, not demand. A walker's hourly income is decided by drive time and cancellations, so the fix is to put demand where the walker already is. What operators really buy is not walks, it is fewer noise complaints and higher pet-owner renewals, so price it against retention, not against Rover.
first_30_days: Start with a building where you already walk two or three dogs. Ask those residents to introduce you to the community manager. Pitch a 60-day pilot at about $750 a month with walk windows and a resident-sign-up QR poster. Measure sign-ups and complaints, then take the numbers to two more buildings in the same operator or neighborhood.

title: Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty
one_liner: A $1 refractometer reading at day 3-5 predicts whether a $1,400 crossbred calf lives, yet nobody independently verifies it at sale. Own that measurement and the warranty that follows.
customer: Calf raisers, backgrounders and feeder buyers who pay a premium for graded calves (or a subscription for the data), and dairies who pay to have calves graded so they can earn the premium. Later, insurers and MGAs underwriting a mortality warranty.
problem: Beef-on-dairy calf output went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to roughly 3.2M in 2024, with CattleFax projecting 5-6M, and calves have sold as high as $1,500 per head. Calf raisers buy 3-5 day old calves nearly blind and eat the 10-25% loss to scours and pneumonia. The colostrum information stays on the dairy, so raisers blame 'bad calves' and dairies blame 'bad luck'. Each dead calf now leaves a four-figure hole in a heifer pipeline that is short by hundreds of thousands of head.
solution: Independent serum total protein (Brix) testing on every calf at day 3-5, done at the dairy or at pickup by trained techs with digital refractometers and a phone app. Each calf is graded on the published four-tier passive-transfer scale (Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor) and logged with dairy, sire, weight and hydration score, then gets a QR tag or passport that follows the calf to the buyer. Buyers pay a premium for Excellent and Good and discount Poor. Phase 2 uses the accumulated data to price a 30- or 60-day mortality warranty ('we have graded 300,000 calves and know what a Brix 8.4 calf from Dairy X does'). Phase 3 gives dairies a colostrum scorecard that brokers use.
why_now: Crossbred calves are at record values, beef-on-dairy volume is doubling, and the heifer shortage means every lost calf is expensive and hard to replace. Consensus passive-transfer grading standards were published in 2020, digital refractometers are cheap, and buyers are already paying for verified genetics programs, so 'verified immunity' is the obvious next tag that nobody sells.
revenue_model: $4-6 per calf grading fee paid by the seller or split with the buyer, then $10-25 per calf warranty premium once loss data supports underwriting (partner with an insurer or MGA rather than carrying risk), plus a data subscription for larger calf raisers and feedlots.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone argues about sire genetics while the vet knows immune status dominates early death, and calves with failure of passive transfer carry about twice the risk of illness and death. The test is $1 and 60 seconds, but a number only has value when a neutral third party holds custody of it at the point of sale. The business is independent custody of the measurement, not the refractometer, and the resulting dataset becomes the underwriting moat.
first_30_days: Two vet techs, two $150 digital refractometers and a phone form. Offer free grading on 5 dairies' weekly calf shipments to 2-3 calf raisers or brokers. Ask the raiser to report 30-day illness and death by calf tag. After about 60 days, publish graded-versus-ungraded outcomes, then get one raiser to commit to a premium (for example $30-50) for Excellent calves and a discount for Poor, and charge the test fee from that point on.

title: Remote Load Calcs That Avoid Panel Upgrades
one_liner: A photo-and-utility-bill service that proves an existing electrical panel can take a heat pump or EV charger, with load-management devices when it cannot.
customer: HVAC and heat-pump contractors, EV-charger installers and solar-plus-storage installers without in-house electricians. Later: state and utility electrification programs.
problem: Data centers are absorbing electricians (nearly a third of the shortage; Texas builders report electrical delays of up to 2 months). Residential electrician time becomes the scarcest input, so panel upgrades stall every electrification job. HVAC contractors selling heat pumps are blocked by work they do not do and cannot schedule. The HVAC rebound expected in 2027 will make it worse.
solution: Installer uploads a photo of the panel label plus 12 months of utility data. The service returns a permit-ready load calculation under the existing-load method, stamped by a remote licensed engineer or electrician. It recommends the cheapest path: no upgrade, a load-management or circuit-pausing device allowed by recent NEC editions, or a smart panel, with the material list for the installer's quote.
why_now: Electrician scarcity from data-center overtime ($130-170K, vendor stat), 2027 HVAC rebound with A2L certification adding friction, and a 110K technician shortage. Load-management devices and energy-management provisions are now commercially available and code-recognized in many places.
revenue_model: $79-149 per calculation billed to installers. Annual contracts with programs. Referral margin from load-management device makers.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for electrification is neither the heat pump nor the HVAC tech, it is the panel and the electrician-days it consumes. Avoiding electrician hours is worth more than adding them, and the existing truck-roll panel check can be done as a $99 desk job by one remote engineer serving many installers.
first_30_days: Sign 20 HVAC contractors in one state. Contract a licensed PE or master electrician for templates and stamps. Deliver 50 calculations by hand. Measure the percentage that avoided an upgrade.

title: Storm-Chaser Livestreams as Claims Evidence
one_liner: License the timestamped, geotagged archives of storm-chaser channels as address-level date-of-loss evidence for hail, wind and flood claims.
customer: Public adjusters, policyholder attorneys and roofing-claim desks in hail states (Colorado, Texas, Nebraska, Minnesota) first. Parametric hail and wind MGAs and appraisal umpires second.
problem: Hail claims turn on whether hail of a given size hit an address on a given date. Radar estimates are error-prone at swath edges, and spotter reports are sparse. Hail drives 26-54% of Colorado premiums (secondary source). Colorado's HB25-1182 (in force since July 2026) and California's AB 75 give owners disclosure and appeal rights, but the evidence burden stays on them ('owners still have to prove their case'). Meanwhile storm chasers stream thousands of hours with GPS, timestamps and hailstones held next to coins, and that ground truth sits unmonetized on YouTube.
solution: Sign revenue-share licenses with chaser channels. Index their archives by time, location and hail size, using computer vision on reference objects, and pair each clip with radar. Sell a 'Date-of-Loss Dossier' per address: nearest verified clips, size estimate, uncertainty and chain of custody. Distribute a printed reference 'hail card' standard to chasers. Add a 'go verify' request queue where adjusters or parametric carriers post bounties on active storms and fans can top them up by tipping.
why_now: Storm-chase livestreaming is now a fan-funded media business with huge live audiences. New state laws create disputes that need evidence. Parametric MGAs need data that cuts basis risk. The 2025-26 hail seasons are still inside claim windows, and the spring 2027 season is six months away, so the archive-first version can sell now.
revenue_model: $39-149 per dossier from public adjusters and roofers, $2-5K a month API access for MGAs and claims shops, and 40-50% revenue share to creators.
non_obvious_insight: The densest hail sensor network in America is a fandom already paid for by fans. Insurers' problem is not data volume but admissible, attributable data, and chasers go exactly to the worst cell. Ground truth is a by-product of entertainment, so the sensor cost is already covered.
first_30_days: Approach 15 mid-size chaser channels (10K-300K subscribers) with a rev-share license for their 2024-26 archives. Index 200 hail events. Sell the first 50 dossiers to 5 Colorado and Texas public adjusters and roofing claim reps for open claims. Draft the reference-card standard for the spring 2027 season.

title: Backflow Testers Roll-Up With Portal-Filing Agents
one_liner: Consolidate small backflow-test shops, then use agents to parse city notices, schedule tests and file results in each water utility's portal, turning mandated annual tests into a low-churn route business.
customer: Property managers, restaurants, car washes, medical buildings, HOAs and multifamily owners who must test backflow assemblies annually, and water utilities who benefit from compliance. Retiring tester shops are the sellers.
problem: Most jurisdictions require annual (sometimes more frequent) tests by a certified tester who submits results to the local water purveyor, and portals and forms vary by utility. Owners miss deadlines and get shutoff threats. Testers are solo or small shops using paper. A failed test triggers repairs worth several times the test fee.
solution: Buy small tester shops to build route density. AI ops: an intake agent parses utility letters and portal notices across a manager's whole portfolio, schedules the nearest tester, files results with browser-automation agents, tracks failures and sends repair quotes. Expand into other mandate-locked recurring routes such as fire extinguisher and sprinkler inspection, kitchen hood, cross-connection surveys and enhanced septic O&M.
why_now: Browser and computer-use agents can now reliably operate idiosyncratic municipal portals. Utilities are moving to online-only submission of test results, and owner-testers are aging out.
revenue_model: $75 to $150 per test, $300 to $1,500 per repair or rebuild, plus annual portfolio management fees for property managers.
non_obvious_insight: A regulator creates the demand and portal friction is the moat. Tests are the loss-leader; repairs, replacements and installs after failed tests carry the margin. Any 'city letter, must act' recurring compliance category is underserved by software, because each authority's process is different.
first_30_days: Start as a compliance concierge for 10 property managers at $15 to $25 per device per year, subcontracting the tests to local certified testers. Build the notice parser and one or two portal integrations. After the flow works, buy one tester shop (about $100k to $250k of owner earnings) on seller financing.
